items.title: Clay Jenkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 18, 2016
items.q: I didn’t hear Milt Jackson making mistakes. And he seemed to be having such a great time.

ctx.x: And that the audience didn’t hear them like they would hear them in a Haydn Trumpet Concerto.

Yes. Because I didn’t hear Milt Jackson making mistakes. And he seemed to be having such a great time. And I’ll tell you something else. I liked — I was brought up in West Texas and it wasn’t a very diverse area racially, but my dad and mom were very open about that, about the beauty of difference in races. And I loved being around African- American people. My dad had some African-American — and I loved that and I loved hearing guys play together and I saw what great friends they were. And I hadn’t seen that…
Yeah. The Kenton band was not like that was it?

items.title: Clay Jenkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 18, 2016
items.q: I heard Milton Jackson, I heard the MJQ, the Modern Jazz Quartet, Ray Brown was playing. And that was pretty amazing. I was just a little kid.

ctx.x: Okay I want you to think back — well I’m not sure when this would be — but did you have a specific moment or moments of inspiration that led you down the jazz path?

Yes. My family was pretty musical and my father played — not professionally but he was a good kind of part time Dixieland trumpet player and he really loved it. And at one time, it was really a moment for me, I was a kid and when he took us to Disneyland — we lived in Texas but we were in California. We went to Disneyland and Stan Kenton’s band was playing. And I was amazed how happy people seemed. And it seemed like heavenly. Everybody was dancing and laughing and talking. And it just seemed like wow, this…
And that the audience didn’t hear them like they would hear them in a Haydn Trumpet Concerto.
